newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain, China to stage HK midnight handover party.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China to stage HK midnight handover party.

text.p: Britain and China signed an agreement on Friday to stage a midnight spectacle of flag changing and renditions of their national anthems when London hands its last major colony back to Beijing's control next year.

The deal, announced by the two countries at the United Nations on Thursday, was signed in Hong Kong by the chief negotiators who have been hammering out the details of the historic sovereignty transfer, set for midnight next June 30.
"Immediately before midnight, the British national anthem will be played as the Union and Hong Kong flags are lowered," the agreement said.

"Immediately after midnight, the Chinese national anthem will be played as the national Flag of the People's Republic of China and the regional flag of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region are raised," it said.
"Appropriate arrangements will be made for dignified and ceremonial departure of the British civilian and military representatives following the ceremony."
Chief British negotiator Hugh Davies told reporters the agreement allowed "normal" press coverage of the ceremony.
News organisations have voiced concern during the past year that China might try to limit press exposure, fearing trouble.

The unprecedented handover of this territory of 6.2 million people will be staged in the foyer of a vast convention centre, with the capacity to seat more than 4,000 people. The building sprawls along Hong Kong's famed Wanchai harbour waterfront.
The agreement ends widespread speculation in Hong Kong on whether China and Britain -- for long at odds over handover details -- would be able to agree on a joint ceremony.
But it was still unclear who would be able to attend the ceremony bringing down the curtains on one and a half centuries of colonial rule in the territory.

The agreement signed on Friday described the ceremony as "solemn and dignified," and to be presided over by senior representatives of Britain and China, with military honour guards, in the presence of a large number of senior dignitaries from overseas governments and international bodies.
China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind discussed the ceremony on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
It had still not been decided who would represent Britain at the ceremony, although Rifkind said Governor Chris Patten would be part of the ceremony.
China has cold-shouldered Patten since 1994 when he expanded direct democracy in Hong Kong's electoral system.
Beijing has vowed to reverse the changes he made and to dismantle the territory's elected legislature upon the handover.
Friday's agreement also specified that Hong Kong police would be responsible for security arrangements at the ceremony.

There had been intense speculation until now in Hong Kong about whether China would want its People's Liberation Army troops, who will garrison the territory after the handover, to supervise the security of Chinese dignitaries at the ceremony.
